newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus leader snubs Russian mediation attempt.
newsitem.headline: Belarus leader snubs Russian mediation attempt.

text.p: Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko on Wednesday snubbed an attempt by Moscow to mediate in his conflict with his opponents and refused to attend proposed peace talks on Russian soil.

Lukashenko spoke for 40 minutes to President Boris Yeltsin, still recovering in hospital after a heart operation two weeks ago, but remained adamant that he would go ahead with a referendum on Sunday to increase his powers.

"The president has decided not to go to Smolensk. He has an extremely tight schedule and so he has decided not to go," Mikhail Podgainy, head of information at the presidential administration, told Reuters.
Asked if his refusal to attend was linked to the fact that his main political opponent, Semyon Sharetsky who heads the parliament, would be there, Podgainy said: "No. The president is very busy."
Lukashenko's closest aide, Vladimir Zametalin, said the president would not be going because Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, expected to attend, would not be there.
Belarussian state television said the two men agreed that they should meet in the near future and that a solution should be found in line with the present constitution and laws.
Interfax news agency quoted Lukashenko as telling deputies loyal to him that his controversial referendum on Sunday would not be scrapped, saying: "There can be no talk of dropping it."

Parliament chairman Semyon Sharetsky, spokesman for the president's opposition, meanwhile left the Belarussian capital to take part in the proposed peace talks with leaders of the two Russian chambers of parliament starting at 1400 GMT in Smolensk, a western Russian city halfway between Moscow and Minsk.

Sharetsky said parliament wanted Lukashenko to cancel the referendum, withdraw his proposed changes to the constitution and a series of decrees, reinstate the sacked head of the Central Electoral Commission and give deputies television time.

"Belarus was once a peaceful, hard-working republic. Now it has been transformed into a battlefield, an arena of hatred. Society is divided, parliament is divided, and the president has set himself against the people and divided society," he said.
Sharetsky's press spokesman told Reuters that Yeltsin, who also spoke to him by telephone, had backed this "zero option" solution, but this could not be confirmed.
Lukashenko, recounting his own telephone talk with the convalescent Russian president, said Yeltsin "admitted he was not sufficiently informed about the real situation in the republic."
Interfax quoted Lukashenko as saying the next step was up to his parliamentary opponents and he would not back down until they withdrew an attempt to impeach him.
Deputy speaker Vasily Novikov made clear after Sharetsky's 10-minute conversation with Yeltsin that deputies would drop threats to impeach Lukashenko if he cancelled the referendum.

But Lukashenko's campaign for the referendum, in which early voting began on November 9, continued apace as the two sides spoke. Loudspeaker were heard in central Minsk, blasting out appeals to the population to vote and support Lukashenko.
A defiant Lukashenko told his critics at a rally on Monday that he would not give up power and they should prepare to "find another motherland" after the referendum.
Lukashenko, who controls the security forces and most of the media and who enjoys considerable support among the mostly rural population of 10 million, has vowed to override any opposition.
His decision to rebuff Russia's mediation attempt appeared to be a slap in the face for the Kremlin, which unlike Western states has avoided criticising him and tried not to take sides.

The 42-year-old leader has scorned Western criticism but is heavily dependent on the political winds blowing from Moscow and needs Russian economic support. He and Yeltsin agreed in April to unite in a "community".
Lukashenko is seeking authority to extend his term by more than two years and widen his powers over all institutions.
